questions.stem: After giving a subcutaneous injection with a safety-engineered needle, which action best follows OSHA sharps-safety requirements?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Activate the safety feature and discard the contaminated needle immediately at the point of use into a closable, puncture-resistant sharps container.","B":"Recap the needle with a one-handed scoop before disposal because this technique is required after routine injections even when no exception applies.","C":"Remove the contaminated needle from the syringe with a mechanical device, then discard the needle and syringe in separate containers to reduce sharps volume.","D":"Carry the used syringe to a central disposal area before activating the safety feature because point-of-use sharps disposal is not necessary."}}
questions.rationale: OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard generally prohibits bending, recapping, removing, shearing, or breaking contaminated needles. Contaminated sharps must be discarded immediately or as soon as feasible into appropriate closable, puncture-resistant, leak-resistant, labeled or color-coded sharps containers located close to the point of use.
questions.source_detail: Contaminated sharps generally must not be recapped and must be discarded immediately or as soon as feasible in proper sharps containers.

questions.stem: After caring for a client with confirmed C. difficile infection, the nurse removes gown and gloves. The nurse's hands are not visibly soiled, and the unit is not experiencing a C. difficile outbreak. Which hand-hygiene action best reflects current CDC guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Skip hand hygiene after leaving the room because intact gloves eliminate the need for cleaning the hands following contact with the client or environment.","B":"Use soap and water because CDC requires soap-and-water washing after every C. difficile encounter regardless of outbreak status or visible soil.","C":"Use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer because CDC still prefers ABHS in most routine clinical situations, including CDI when hands are not visibly soiled.","D":"Use chlorhexidine surgical scrub because routine alcohol hand sanitizer and ordinary soap are both contraindicated after contact with C. difficile spores."}}
questions.rationale: CDC currently prefers alcohol-based hand sanitizer in most clinical situations when hands are not visibly soiled, and states that this preference does not change solely because the patient has C. difficile infection. Soap and water is indicated when hands are visibly soiled and is encouraged as an additional precaution during C. difficile outbreaks.
questions.source_name: CDC — Clinical Safety: Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers
questions.source_detail: ABHS remains preferred in most routine clinical situations, including CDI when hands are not visibly soiled; soap and water is emphasized for visible soil and CDI outbreaks.

questions.stem: A Mantoux tuberculin skin test is placed Monday at 10:00. Which follow-up instruction is correct?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Return one week later because delayed hypersensitivity cannot be interpreted reliably until at least seven days after the test is placed.","B":"Return between Wednesday 10:00 and Thursday 10:00 so a trained clinician can measure induration during the required 48–72-hour window.","C":"Return Monday evening because the result is determined by the amount of redness that develops during the first six to twelve hours.","D":"Photograph the site at 24 hours and send the image because visual redness is sufficient to determine whether a tuberculin skin test is positive."}}
questions.rationale: CDC guidance requires a tuberculin skin test to be read by a trained healthcare worker 48 to 72 hours after placement. The reader measures induration in millimeters, not erythema. A Monday 10:00 placement should therefore be read between Wednesday 10:00 and Thursday 10:00.
questions.source_name: CDC — Clinical Testing Guidance for Tuberculosis: Tuberculin Skin Test
questions.source_detail: Read the TST 48–72 hours after placement; measure induration, not erythema.

questions.stem: A nurse sustains a hollow-bore needlestick from a patient whose HIV status is not immediately available. After washing the site, which action is the priority?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Wait for the source patient's final laboratory result before reporting the exposure because treatment decisions should not begin until infection is confirmed.","B":"Monitor for fever or rash for several days and seek care only if symptoms appear because post-exposure treatment is unnecessary before symptoms develop.","C":"Schedule routine employee-health testing for the following week because occupational HIV exposure is not considered time-sensitive when source status is unknown.","D":"Report the exposure and obtain urgent medical evaluation for PEP; when indicated, treatment should start as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours."}}
questions.rationale: CDC treats potential HIV exposure as time-sensitive. Occupational exposures should be reported and medically evaluated immediately. When PEP is indicated, it should be started as soon as possible and no later than 72 hours after exposure; source testing should not create unnecessary delay in evaluation.
questions.source_name: CDC — Preventing HIV with PEP / 2025 Occupational Exposure Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Healthcare workers should report occupational exposures and seek medical attention immediately; PEP must begin within 72 hours and sooner is better.

questions.stem: An indwelling urinary catheter is being inserted in an acute-care hospital. Which technique best reflects CDC CAUTI-prevention guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Perform hand hygiene and insert the catheter aseptically using sterile gloves, a sterile catheter kit, and a single-use lubricant packet.","B":"Use sterile gloves and a sterile catheter but clean lubricant because the urethral meatus is colonized and cannot be made completely sterile.","C":"Use clean gloves with a sterile catheter kit because only the catheter itself needs to remain sterile during insertion in an acute-care setting.","D":"Use sterile insertion technique but disconnect the drainage tubing briefly after placement to verify urine flow before closing the system"}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends that acute-care urinary catheters be inserted using aseptic technique and sterile equipment. Recommended supplies include sterile gloves, drape and sponges, appropriate antiseptic or sterile solution for periurethral cleaning, and a single-use lubricant packet. A closed drainage system should then be maintained.
questions.source_detail: In acute care, use aseptic insertion and sterile equipment, including sterile gloves and a single-use lubricant packet.
